summary.one_line: A five-year-old Gurugram MICE/incentive-travel organiser with ~₹100 cr of largely pass-through revenue, 86% of it from banking and insurance clients and 43% from a single customer, raising ₹38.12 cr (all fresh) mainly to fund a receivables build-up and repay debt; profits are rising, but cash flow is negative and the governance record is patchy. Avoid.
bull_points: PAT more than doubled from ₹3.29 cr (FY24) to ₹7.72 cr (FY26), and EBITDA margin widened from 4.77% to 10.22% as the company moved to larger, international assignments (S11, S18).
Events billed at ₹50 lakh or more rose from 31 in FY25 to 49 in FY26, 23 of them international. That is some evidence of moving up the ticket-size ladder (S18).
The issue is 100% fresh with no offer for sale, so all ₹38.12 cr goes to the company and no promoter is selling (S2, S5).
Customer concentration improved in FY26: the top customer's share fell from 63.21% (FY24) to 42.72%, and the top-10 share from 96.67% (FY25) to 84.59% (S18).
The model is asset-light (no venues or fleet owned) and runs with 35 employees, so there is little capex burden (S11, S6).
bear_points: Extreme concentration: one customer supplied 42.72% of FY26 revenue, the top 10 supplied 84.59%, and insurance and banking together supplied 85.91% (S18, S19).

Operating cash flow was negative in FY25 (−₹2.89 cr) and FY26 (−₹4.52 cr) while PAT was ₹5.13 cr and ₹7.72 cr. Trade receivables tripled to ₹29.87 cr, and receivable days stretched from 37 to 73 (S20, S9).
About ₹25.8 cr of the ₹27.2 cr in specified objects goes to working capital and debt repayment. The IPO mostly refinances the cash gap the business creates rather than building new capacity (S5, S9).
Compliance history: RoC filings delayed by up to 477 days, past auditor observations on EPF/ESI and GST compliance, and a promoter previously a director of a company under strike-off (S6, S17).
The promoters run a proprietary firm, also called M/s Eventions. A non-compete with it was signed only on March 30, 2026, just before the DRHP (S6).
watch_points: Whether the top customer (42.72% of FY26 revenue) is retained and whether FY27 receivable days come down toward the 65 days assumed in the working-capital plan (S18, S9).
Execution and cash burn at Gantu Online, the 70% subsidiary bought from the promoters that gets ₹1.40 cr for a B2C travel portal (S10).
Final subscription figures at close on October 5, 2026. No category-wise figures were published at the time of writing (S11).
Unbilled revenue of ₹20.50 cr at FY26 (20.55% of revenue) and how quickly it converts to cash (S20, S6).

reasoning: The money plugs a cash gap rather than funding growth. Of the ₹27.20 cr in specified objects, ₹18.80 cr is working capital and ₹7.00 cr is debt repayment (S5, S11). Working capital needs rose from ₹3.92 cr (FY24) to ₹23.99 cr (FY26) because receivable days doubled to 73 (S9). Investors would be financing the float the company extends to its clients.

There is no durable moat. Eventions is essentially a contract designer and logistics aggregator (S6). Cost of services absorbs roughly 80–85% of revenue (S6), and it competes with Thomas Cook/SOTC, Cox & Kings, Wizcraft and many unorganised DMCs (S6). Nothing in the filing points to proprietary technology, a regulatory licence barrier or a market-share claim that would stop a large client from switching.

The business depends heavily on a few clients in one sector. One customer is 42.72% of revenue, the top 10 are 84.59% (S18), and banking and insurance are 85.91% (S19). The investing.com analysis flags possible caps on insurance distribution spending as a sector risk (S6). Losing one relationship could wipe out most of the profit growth shown.

Earnings are not converting to cash. Cumulative FY25–FY26 PAT was about ₹12.9 cr, while operating cash flow was about −₹7.4 cr over the same years (S20, S11). Unbilled revenue jumped from ₹4.62 cr to ₹20.50 cr (S20). Until receivables normalise, the reported margin expansion is partly an accrual story.

Governance quality is below what a small, 99.96%-promoter-owned company needs to earn outside trust. There were RoC filing delays of up to 477 days, past auditor qualifications on EPF/ESI and GST, and a pending GNL-1 adjudication filing (S6, S17). The promoters also sold their Gantu stake to the company for shares in March 2026 (S10, S16), and a same-named promoter proprietorship was only bound by a non-compete in March 2026 (S6).

subsections.title: What Eventions actually does and how it earns money

blocks.text: Eventions Limited was incorporated on December 15, 2020 in Gurugram, Haryana. It converted from a private to a public company, and changed its name from Eventions Private Limited, on February 26, 2026 (S13, S25). It plans and runs corporate events: incentive trips for a client's sales force, delegate conferences, meetings, exhibitions and brand activations, in India and overseas (S1, S5). It owns no venues, hotels or vehicles. For each project it books and coordinates hotels, destination management companies (DMCs), airlines, logistics firms and production vendors, then bills the client for the full package (S5, S6).

Fees are either fixed turnkey prices or cost-plus margins. Revenue is recognised when the event is completed or at contractual milestones (S6). Because the invoice includes the third-party costs of flights, rooms and venues, the top line is largely pass-through: the investing.com analysis puts cost of services at roughly 80–85% of operating revenue (S6). The company's real economic output is the gap between what it charges and what it pays vendors. In FY26 that was an EBITDA of about ₹10.2 cr on ₹99.74 cr of operating revenue (S11, S18).

A typical project runs like this. A banking or insurance client commissions an incentive trip for its top-performing agents. Eventions designs the itinerary, pays advances to hotels and DMCs, then runs the event on the ground. Final billing often waits for multi-stage cost finalisation, customer approvals and third-party validation of reimbursable expenses (S20). The company therefore pays out cash first and collects later. This drives the working-capital pattern discussed in the financials section (S9).

Revenue here is gross event billing, not value added. ₹100 cr of 'revenue' is closer to ₹15–20 cr of gross margin (cost of services ~80–85% per S6). Judge the business on margin and cash, not on the top line.

subsections.title: Revenue mix: services, sectors and geography

blocks.caption: Revenue mix by service line and client sector (share of operating revenue)

blocks.text: Sources: S18, S19. n/d = not disclosed in the sources reviewed. MICE, mostly incentive travel and conferences for financial-services clients, is the whole business. Corporate events are a secondary line, and the FIT (free independent traveller) business run through the new subsidiary Gantu Online is negligible so far (S18). By client sector the dependence is even starker. Insurance and banking accounted for 86–89% of revenue in every year shown, and FMCG was a distant second at about 6% (S19).

By geography, international assignments rose from 62.31% of revenue in FY25 to 71.10% (₹70.91 cr) in FY26 (S19). The company lists destinations including Spain, France, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Hungary, the UAE, Azerbaijan, Singapore and Indonesia (S15, S22). The count of high-value events (billed at ₹50 lakh or more) grew from 31 in FY25 (16 international, 9 long-haul) to 49 in FY26 (23 international, 17 long-haul). Management credits this shift for its margin expansion (S18). Chanakyanipothi counts 107 such events across FY24–FY26 (S12), and other reviews cite more than 200 events of all sizes over the same period (S14).
More international work widens margins but also raises foreign-exchange exposure, advance payments to overseas vendors and receivable days. All three show up in the FY26 balance sheet (S9, S20).

blocks.caption: Customer concentration (share of revenue from operations)

blocks.text: Source: S18. The customers are not named in the sources reviewed. Given the sector split, the largest is almost certainly a bank or insurer (S19). Concentration eased meaningfully in FY26, but a single client still supplies more than two-fifths of revenue. The RHP itself describes the business as deriving a significant portion of revenue from a limited number of customers, much of it repeat engagements, and says any reduction could materially affect results (S17, S5). The work is project-based rather than contracted recurring revenue (S18).

On the supply side, delivery depends on hotels, DMCs, logistics providers and production vendors (S5). The RHP flags partner performance and coordination as an execution risk (S5). The sources reviewed give no supplier-concentration figures. Operating scale is small: 35 employees as of March 31, 2026 (S11), one registered office at Plot 108, Sector 44, Gurgaon (S3), and total assets of ₹50.63 cr at FY26 (S11).

Subsidiary: Eventions bought 70% of Gantu Online Private Limited on March 10, 2026 from its own promoters (S10). Gantu was incorporated on August 30, 2024 and targets B2C free-independent-traveller leisure trips. The plan is to use it to convert corporate incentive travellers into retail customers (S10, S6). It contributed 0.11% of FY26 revenue (S18).

Market-size estimates for Indian MICE vary so widely that none should be relied on. IMARC puts the market at USD 116.0 bn in 2025, growing to USD 184.8 bn by 2034 at a 5.04% CAGR (S23). Mordor Intelligence values MICE tourism at USD 37.75 bn in 2025 (S26). MarketsandData estimates only USD 5.42 bn in FY2025, growing at 6.67% (S27). Preqt, citing an industry source, gives USD 5.2 bn (2024) to USD 7.8 bn (2029) at 8.3% CAGR for events and exhibitions (S14). The investing.com analysis sizes Eventions' addressable market at ₹30,000–40,000 cr, with a serviceable segment of ₹8,000–12,000 cr growing 8–11% (S6).

What matters for an investor is that the addressable pool, however defined, is huge relative to a ₹100 cr company. Growth is therefore about winning clients, not about the market. Demand drivers cited include corporate incentive budgets, professionally managed conferences, post-COVID recovery in international travel and the government's 'Meet in India' push (S6, S14). The same sources flag the downside: MICE spending is discretionary and is among the first budgets cut in a downturn (S6).
The industry reports differ by more than 20x (USD 5 bn vs USD 116 bn) because of definitional differences (S23, S27). Treat any single market-size figure in marketing material with scepticism.

subsections.title: Competitors and whether there is a moat

blocks.text: Listed companies cited as comparable include Touchwood Entertainment, Thomas Cook (India), Yatra Online and Easy Trip Planners. Unlisted competitors include Cox & Kings, SOTC Travel, Creative Travel, Wizcraft, Event Graphia and many regional DMCs (S6). The RHP also names competition from organised, unorganised and tech-enabled entrants, plus international MICE destinations such as Singapore, the UAE and Thailand competing for the same budgets (S5).

The company's stated strengths are an execution track record, experienced promoters, an asset-light scalable model, capability for large-format events, and client-centric repeat business (S3, S17). These are generic claims. No source reviewed reports a market-share claim, an exclusive supplier arrangement, a licence or regulatory barrier, or proprietary technology. The only real asset is the relationship with a handful of insurance and banking clients (S18, S19). That is valuable while it lasts but is not a moat, because clients can and do rebid incentive programmes. The investing.com analysis explicitly lists disintermediation, meaning large clients contracting vendors directly, as a risk (S6).

items: Advantage: niche expertise in insurance and banking incentive travel, with year-on-year repeat work from the same clients (S5, S19).
Advantage: asset-light, so growth needs working capital rather than fixed assets (S6).
No moat: low switching costs, pass-through pricing and vendor-price volatility that can squeeze turnkey margins (S6).
No moat: limited brand equity compared with Thomas Cook/SOTC and other large travel groups (S6).

blocks.text: Plain conclusion: Eventions has no structural moat. Its position rests on a few client relationships, most of all one client that supplies 42.72% of revenue (S18).

blocks.caption: Restated consolidated financials, ₹ crore (FY ending March 31)

blocks.text: Sources: total income, EBITDA and PAT from S11 and S15, matching S2 and S22; revenue from operations from S13 and S18; margins from S18; finance costs from S20. Anand Rathi shows a different EBITDA series (₹4.85/7.58/11.07 cr) (S3), probably because it includes other income. This report uses the ₹4.13/7.09/10.19 cr series, which four sources agree on. Screener-style data on StockScans also shows FY23 revenue of about ₹42 cr and PAT of about ₹1 cr (S4). Those figures fall outside the restated three-year window and are indicative only.

Revenue was essentially flat from FY24 to FY25 (+0.8%) and grew about 14% in FY26 (S14, S8). The two-year revenue CAGR is about 7.3% (S14), not a high-growth profile. The real story is margins. EBITDA margin more than doubled, which management attributes to 'a favourable event mix, including more premium, higher-ticket and international assignments' (S18). That explanation is plausible, but mix-driven gains are not locked in: losing a few large overseas programmes would reverse them. The RHP itself warns that recent PAT margins may not be sustainable (S17).

subsections.title: Balance sheet, working capital and cash flow

blocks.text: Sources: S11 (assets, net worth, borrowings); S20 (receivables, unbilled revenue, operating cash flow; S13 and S14 give matching rounded operating cash flow of +0.3/−2.9/−4.5); S9 (days and working-capital requirement). The sources report unbilled revenue separately from receivables and do not make clear whether it is included in the receivables figure.

This is the weakest part of the story. Profits rose each year, but operating cash flow turned negative in FY25 and fell further in FY26 (S20). In FY26 trade receivables rose by about ₹20 cr and working capital absorbed about ₹13 cr (S20). Receivable days doubled from 37 to 73, while the company pays vendors in 13–16 days (S9). In other words, Eventions is financing its clients: it prepays hotels and DMCs, then waits two to three months to be paid. The gap has been funded by short-term borrowings, which rose to ₹9.44 cr at rates of 9–19%, and by retained profits (S20, S9). Debt-to-equity was 0.52 at FY26 (S20). Debt is not yet high in absolute terms, but it is rising quickly.

Net worth rose from ₹9.86 cr to ₹18.13 cr in FY26. Most of that was retained PAT of ₹7.72 cr, plus a rights issue of 4.9 lakh shares at ₹10 (about ₹0.49 cr) and a share swap for Gantu (S16, S11). Return on equity of 55.16% in FY26 (S7, S14) looks high because the equity base is tiny. It is not evidence of a capital-light compounder.

Cash-flow/profit mismatch: FY25–FY26 cumulative PAT was about ₹12.9 cr, while operating cash flow over the same two years was about −₹7.4 cr (S11, S20). Unbilled revenue more than quadrupled in two years (S20). This is the red flag an investor should weigh most.

subsections.title: Does the trend support the growth story?

blocks.text: Only partly. The margin trend is real and consistent across sources (S11, S18). Revenue growth, however, has been modest (flat in FY25, +14% in FY26) (S14), and the FY26 improvement came with a sharp rise in receivables and unbilled revenue (S20). In a pass-through business, a quick way to show higher growth and margins is to take larger client programmes on longer credit terms. The balance sheet shows exactly that pattern (S9, S20).

items: Supports the story: the FY26 fall in customer concentration shows new logos being added (top-10 share down from 96.67% to 84.59%) (S18).
Supports the story: more premium, international high-ticket events (49 vs 31) (S18).

Undermines it: the RHP's own working-capital plan assumes receivable days fall to 65 and that short-term borrowings drop to zero once IPO money arrives (S9). That is a forecast, not a demonstrated trend.
Undermines it: finance costs rose 70% in FY26, from ₹39.23 lakh to ₹66.75 lakh (S20).

blocks.text: Some secondary sources print obvious unit errors, for example operating cash flow of '−₹451.75 crore' (S6) where the correct figure is ₹451.75 lakh (S20). This report uses figures cross-checked across at least two sources.

The split between general corporate purposes and issue expenses is not disclosed in the sources reviewed, and is not guessed here. No definitive agreement or purchase order has been placed, and the quotes exclude GST (S10).

subsections.title: What the money actually does for shareholders

blocks.text: The IPO does not fund capacity, acquisitions or a new product in any material way. About 95% of the specified objects (₹25.80 cr of ₹27.20 cr) goes to funding receivables and repaying the short-term debt that was itself taken to fund receivables (S5, S9, S20). The RHP's working-capital plan projects that, with IPO money, short-term borrowings fall to zero by March 2027 and March 2028 while the working-capital requirement rises to ₹33.17 cr by FY28 (S9).

items: Positive: all proceeds go to the company with no OFS, and deleveraging cuts interest costs of 9–19% (S2, S20).
Neutral: working-capital funding is a legitimate need for this model, but it only adds value if the float earns more than it costs. That depends on collections improving (S9).
Negative: ₹1.40 cr goes to a promoter-originated subsidiary with minimal revenue and only quotations behind it (S10, S18).

blocks.text: The 100% fresh issue is a genuine plus. But investors are mainly funding the company's credit to its clients, not a growth asset.

blocks.caption: Promoter shareholding before the issue
rows: Whole-time Director & CEO (called MD in the company press release)

blocks.text: Sources: S16 (shareholding); S6 and S13 (roles); S15 and S21 (the press release describes Ravi Rajak as Managing Director). Cristoo Arora has about 15 years of MICE/events experience. Ravi Rajak comes from tourism and travel, with 7+ years of experience per Preqt (S6, S14). Kirat Ahluwalia brings marketing and brand expertise (S6). The company secretary and compliance officer is Misha Dhawan (S6). No promoter pledge is reported (S14).

Track record: the promoters have run this company only since December 2020 (S13), alongside a proprietary firm, M/s Eventions, in the same line of business (S6). Ravi Rajak was previously a director of Aadvik Traders Private Limited, which is under the process of being struck off by the RoC. The RHP discloses this as a risk factor (S6, S17). The board has five directors, two of them independent, and both independents were appointed in February 2026, just before filing (S14).

Capital history is worth noting. The promoters built their 99.96% stake at essentially face value: a 1:49 bonus and a rights issue at ₹10 in September 2025, then a 1:8 bonus in March 2026 (S16). New shareholders are paying ₹112–118 for shares whose bonus-adjusted cost to the promoters is a small fraction of that (S16, S1).

items: Gantu Online acquisition (March 10, 2026): Eventions bought 70% of Gantu from Cristo Arora and Ravi Rajak, who are promoters of both companies. It paid by issuing 43,509 Eventions shares at ₹15.55 each (S10, S16). The company is now putting ₹1.40 cr of IPO money into this same entity (S10).

M/s Eventions proprietorship: the promoters' proprietary firm shares the company's name and business. An indefinite non-compete was signed only on March 30, 2026. It requires competing corporate B2B enquiries to be routed to the listed company, with a penalty of three times the revenue from any breach (S6). The RHP separately flags conflicts because promoter-group entities are or may be in a similar business (S17).
Loans and imprest: gross FY26 related-party movements, including loans, repayments and imprest (cash advances), were about ₹9.4 cr, roughly 9.4% of revenue (S14).

blocks.text: This is not a routine RPT section. The ₹9.4 cr of FY26 related-party flows, if the gross figure is accurate, is large relative to ₹18 cr of net worth (S14, S11). The reviewed sources do not break it down by counterparty or state the closing balances, so it is unclear how much is a genuine loan relationship and how much is travel imprest. The Gantu deal and the same-named proprietorship were tidied up only in the weeks before the DRHP was filed (S10, S6). That fits a pattern of cleaning up the structure for listing rather than a long record of arm's-length dealing.

Main RPT concern: a promoter-owned firm with the same name, in the same business, bound only by a March 2026 contract (S6). Investors must rely on that contract being enforced to keep business flowing to the listed company.

items: RoC filing delays: Form INC-20A (declaration of commencement of business) was filed 477 days late, Form ADT-1 (auditor appointment) 355 days late and Form AOC-4 (financial statements) 343 days late (S6).
Voluntary adjudication: Form GNL-1 was filed on March 31, 2026 in connection with commencing business before completing the required filings under Section 10A(1) of the Companies Act (S6).

Auditor observations: FY24 audit reports flagged EPF/ESI contribution lapses and a suo motu GST registration cancellation in Kerala, with ₹8.22 lakh of unpaid interest provided for (S6). The RHP has a risk factor on past auditor qualifications and adverse observations (S17).
Litigation: a pending consumer complaint and ongoing tax proceedings. No criminal or SEBI proceedings are reported (S14).

blocks.text: No single item is severe in isolation, and the pending matters are small. Together, though, they describe a founder-run firm that did not keep basic statutory compliance in order until an IPO forced it to (S6, S17). The recently formed committees and newly appointed compliance officer (S6) have no track record yet.

Governance verdict: below average for an SME IPO. Year-long filing lapses, promoter-linked structural transactions just before filing, and a board whose independent directors are months old (S6, S14).

items: Single-client dependence: the top customer supplied 42.72% of FY26 revenue and 63.21% in FY24 (S18). Losing or re-tendering this account would probably erase most of the company's profit.

Sector dependence: 85.91% of revenue comes from insurance and banking clients (S19). A regulatory curb on insurance distribution or incentive spending, which investing.com flags as a risk, would hit almost the whole book at once (S6).

Working capital and collections: receivable days of 73, ₹20.50 cr of unbilled revenue and two years of negative operating cash flow (S9, S20). A delayed payment from a top client could stress liquidity even after the IPO.

Margin sustainability: the EBITDA margin rose to 10.22% on event mix, not contracted pricing (S18). The RHP warns that recent PAT margins may not be sustainable (S17). Vendor price inflation on fixed-price turnkey contracts compresses margins directly (S6).
Discretionary demand and currency: MICE budgets are cut early in a downturn, and 71% international revenue exposes margins to INR depreciation and to travel-safety events (S6, S19).

blocks.text: These five risks are linked. A few large financial-services clients take longer credit on bigger overseas programmes. That lifts margins but also lifts receivables and debt (S9, S18, S20). If the model runs in reverse, with a client lost or a delayed payment, profit and cash would fall together.

items: Promoter conflict: a same-named promoter proprietorship operates in the same business under a non-compete dated March 30, 2026 (S6, S17).
Gantu execution: an early-stage B2C travel subsidiary with limited history, bought from the promoters and funded by IPO money on the strength of vendor quotes only (S10, S4).
Compliance record: past RoC delays, auditor qualifications and a promoter linked to a company being struck off could attract regulatory scrutiny (S6, S17).
SME liquidity: the stock will trade on NSE Emerge with a market maker and large minimum lots (1,200 shares), so exiting can be hard in a weak market (S2, S12).

blocks.text: Lock-in: 25,00,000 promoter shares are designated as the minimum promoter contribution and locked in for three years from allotment. The remaining pre-issue promoter shares follow a one-year and two-year lock-in schedule (S16). This is shorter than for mainboard issues. Since promoters hold 99.96% before the issue, most of their stake becomes free to trade within one to two years of listing (S16, S2).
No material litigation threatens the business (S14). The risks that matter are commercial (concentration, collections) and governance, not legal.

Management's public statements are generic. Ravi Rajak says the IPO 'will strengthen our financial foundation, support our working capital needs and help us further build our capabilities' (S1, S15). He also says Eventions has built its business 'by bringing MICE services and event management together under one platform' (S21). The sources reviewed contain no revenue or margin guidance, no investor call and no interview with specific targets.

The concrete plans in the offer document are: (1) keep scaling larger, premium and international assignments, which management credits for recent margin gains (S18); (2) build a B2C travel portal through Gantu to convert corporate incentive travellers into retail customers (S10, S6); and (3) retire short-term debt and fund working capital from IPO money (S9).
There is no explicit growth guidance. Any growth outlook comes from the working-capital projections below, which are planning assumptions made for sizing the IPO, not targets.

subsections.title: Projections embedded in the working-capital plan

blocks.caption: RHP working-capital assessment: actual vs projected

blocks.text: Source: S9. The plan implies a working-capital need about 40% higher in FY28 than in FY27, which suggests management expects meaningful business growth in FY28. It also assumes collections improve (65 vs 73 days) and that internal accruals of ₹23.37 cr are available in FY28 (S9). That accrual figure is about three times FY26 PAT (S11), so the plan assumes strong profit growth that has not yet been shown.

items: Watch: whether H1 FY27 receivable days actually fall toward 65 (S9).
Watch: whether operating cash flow turns positive once IPO money replaces bank debt (S20).
Watch: whether Gantu produces revenue or only consumes cash (S10, S18).

subsections.title: Status at the time of writing (day 1, September 30, 2026)

blocks.text: The issue opened on September 30, 2026, the date of this report, and closes on October 5 (S1, S11). No category-wise subscription figures (retail/NII/QIB) had been published on the sources checked (Chittorgarh, IIFL, Multibagg) at the time of writing (S11, S7, S28). Any demand signal is therefore absent, not merely partial.

Anchor investors: Chittorgarh lists an anchor date of September 29, 2026 (S24), but no anchor allocation, investor names or amount had been disclosed in any source reviewed (S11, S7). Chittorgarh's reservation table allots only 1,62,000 shares (about ₹1.9 cr) to QIBs in total (S11), so any anchor book would be very small. Under SME norms anchor shares carry a lock-in, but no Eventions-specific anchor lock-in was confirmed.

Grey market premium (unofficial): several platforms reported a GMP of ₹0 on September 26–28, 2026, implying no expected listing gain (S2, S5, S8). GMP is unregulated, thinly traded and is not an investment signal. It is recorded here only for completeness and plays no part in the verdict.
Check NSE's live bid details before the October 5 close. Day-1 SME books are typically dominated by the NII and retail categories and say little about final demand.

method: Research was done on 2026-09-30 using web search and page fetches. The primary documents could not be read directly. The Eventions DRHP on NSE archives (S25, file dated March 31, 2026) was found, but two fetch attempts timed out. The final RHP on the company website (eventions.in) refused connections, and downloading it via shell was not permitted in this environment. So no figure in this report comes from reading the offer document itself. Instead, RHP-derived data was taken from secondary sources that quote the RHP directly: Multibagg's RHP-based articles for customer concentration, sector mix, working capital, cash flow, capital history and Gantu; the investing.com analysis for RPTs and compliance; Chittorgarh, a2zipo, DSIJ, Goodreturns and the company press release for issue terms and financials. Each material figure was cross-checked against at least two sources where possible. Total income, EBITDA, PAT, net worth and borrowings agree across four or more sources. Customer concentration, cash flow, receivables and the working-capital plan come mainly from Multibagg (S9, S18, S19, S20), and for cash flow are corroborated by ICICI Direct and Preqt (S13, S14). RoC filing-delay details (477/355/343 days) come from investing.com (S6), and the fact of RoC delays is corroborated by INDmoney and Preqt (S17, S14). The ₹9.4 cr related-party figure comes only from Preqt (S14) and could not be broken down. Known conflicts: EBITDA per Anand Rathi (S3) differs from the four-source consensus; reservation percentages differ across platforms, and Chittorgarh's share counts were used; Ravi Rajak's title (MD vs Whole-time Director & CEO) differs between the press release and analyst notes; investing.com contains unit errors, which were corrected against Multibagg. Material gaps: customer and supplier names, the split between general corporate purposes and issue expenses, a counterparty breakdown of RPTs, and anchor allocation and subscription data (not yet published). The task brief said the price band was not yet known, but the ₹112–118 band was widely reported, including in the company release, so it is included. Valuation (P/E, peer multiples) is deliberately excluded, and multiples volunteered by sources were omitted. The verdict does not use GMP or subscription data.
